News.title: Behind the scenes chaos during Trump’s visit to Beijing as staffer trampled & row between elite Secret Services erupts
News.content:
TENSIONS are boiling behind the scenes on Donald Trump’s visit to Beijing as physical rows erupted between Chinese officials and White House aides.

Fierce arguments have marred the high stakes crunch-talks – one fight even left a US staffer trampled by a horde of Chinese journalists.





A member of the US delegation was heard blasting the backstage bust-ups as a “s***show”.

The first of several skirmishes started on Thursday morning when a pack of Chinese press stormed into Trump’s meeting with President Xi.

The crowd knocked over and then stepped on a White House staffer, sparking loud protests from the Americans.

The unnamed aide was bruised and shaken, but thankfully not seriously injured.



The chaos continued mere hours later when Chinese officials refused to allow a US Secret Service agent to enter UNESCO world-heritage site the Temple of Heaven.

The agent was carrying a firearm and had been sent to protect the press.



A tense standoff ensued between the US press and Beijing officials.

“We’re in the motorcade with the President, do you not understand that?” one reporter admonished the Chinese.

A tense 30 minutes later another Secret Service agent – who had been cleared beforehand – accompanied the reporters inside.



While President Xi and Donald Trump peacefully enjoyed a tour of the historic temple, off stage relations between the Chinese and US delegations continued to sour.

American reporters were shut inside a holding room for the duration of the presidential tour.

And then when the time came to rejoin the presidential motorcade, Beijing officers barred the way.

“We have to go!” cried one US journalist whilst another White House official told the Chinese that the Trump administration would never treat them this way.

When the press finally broke out, one woman is heard saying: “Do not run over anybody, do not do what they did to us”, in reference to the Chinese press trampling a staffer earlier that day.



In a bizarre twist, the entire showdown was captured on film by director Brett Ratner – who produced the first lady’s documentary Melania.

Ratner was in China preparing to shoot Rush Hour 4.

The Asian superpower is a under a dictatorship however and press reports are tightly monitored by the state.

Chinese officials chased the US delegation as they ran across the square to reach Trump’s convoy of cars.



Relations between the two countries are often on a rollercoaster.

In a post on May 13 the US president hailed President Xi as a “Leader of extraordinary distinction”.

But he has previously accused the nation of a cover up over the coronavirus pandemic and slammed them for not stopping the spread sooner.

The Sun exclusively witnessed the moment that Trump confronted Xi over the deadly disease.



President Xi also issued an ominous warning during the diplomatic visit, saying that the US faces a “highly dangerous situation” if the relationship is ruined.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

During a two-hour showdown earlier on Thursday Xi said: “If handled properly, bilateral relations can remain generally stable.

“If handled poorly, the two countries will clash or even come into conflict, pushing the entire China-US relationship into a highly dangerous situation.”

News.title: Young ‘gang rape victim’ leaps from balcony ‘trying to flee attackers’ leaving her with traumatic brain injuries
News.content:
DESPERATE ESCAPE Young ‘gang rape victim’ leaps from balcony ‘trying to flee attackers’ leaving her with traumatic brain injuries

A YOUNG woman has been left with traumatic brain injuries after leaping off a balcony while allegedly trying to escape being gang raped, reports say.

The alleged victim plummeted from the first floor of an apartment while trying to flee the suspects – with police launching an investigation into the ordeal.





Emergency services rushed to the scene of the fall after being alerted that a woman had plunged from a balcony.

The fire department raced to Senftenberger Straße at 3:15am on Tuesday before finding the woman in horrific condition.

She had reportedly been helped back inside her apartment by five unidentified men.

When ambulances arrived, her condition is said to have been so severe that an emergency physician vehicle was called in.

Police also came to the scene and launched a probe shortly after – but no arrests have been made.

After the woman was rushed to hospital, doctors found she had suffered traumatic brain injuries.

She is currently receiving treatment.

Police sources told Bild that a possible sexual offence inside the apartment was being investigated.



Searches have been carried out in the property as part of the investigation.

On Wednesday, forensic inspectors came to the scene to collect samples from the apartment.

But police have not ruled out the possibility that the alleged suspects may have attempted to destroy evidence.

News.title: Inside child phone capital of UK, where 90% of kids have mobile as ‘babysitter’ & spend six hours a day on screens
News.content:
MUMS spill out of cafes in a bustling city centre and chat happily while their toddlers are occupied in their buggies.

But instead of toys or teddies to keep the children entertained, these youngsters have phones in their tiny hands — and their attention is fixed firmly on the screen in front of them.



It’s a common sight here in ­Newcastle, where more children have phones than anywhere else in the UK — and where some mums tell us they see them as babysitters.

In this city, 90.5 per cent of eight to 11-year-olds own one, compared with the national average of 61 per cent.

Newcastle has been dubbed the smartphone capital of the UK for kids — and some experts are calling for better education for parents.



Excessive screen time among children has been linked to developmental delay, poor social skills and obesity.

Wrangling her three young kids to a bus stop, Jade Owen laughs: “It feels as though they were born with screens in their hands.”

The 30-year-old mum says that phones and iPads are an integral part of her kids’ lives. Two of her children — autistic Lennox, ten, and Colby-Lee, six — rack up nine hours of screen time a day between them.

Jade said: “Lennox must spend around six hours a day on screens and that’s OK with me because he’s happy and he’s occupied.

“When I was his age I was outside playing with my friends most of the time, but apart from the telly there was nothing to stay in for.



“I don’t think it’s safe for children to play out now — not where we live.”

But Jade, from the city’s deprived Benwell suburb, insisted she has things under control.

She said: “I know what Lennox is watching because his phone is linked to my phone. I know that the things he watches are decent and appropriate and I know he’s safe.

“Colby-Lee is on screens for three hours and likes to spend time on Roblox (a gaming platform) talking to his friends. I keep a close eye on that as well.”



As 18-month-old daughter Isla lay napping in her pushchair, Jade said with a laugh: “She does love to watch the telly.

“Screens keep all three of them occupied so I can get things done around the house.”

Excessive phone use among kids is an issue that the whole country will be more than familiar with.

Despite recent Government guidelines that parents should avoid screen time for kids under two, new research conducted by children’s charity the 1001 Critical Days ­Foundation found two-thirds of kids in that age range regularly use devices with screens.



And shockingly, one in ten babies now regularly fall asleep with a screen in their cot.

The report found the jump in screen time led to reduced interaction between babies and adults which is “central” to the risks observed.

These include increased chance of obesity and short-sightedness, sleep difficulties, behavioural difficulties, language delay and later challenges with friendships.

It added the developmental risks associated with screen use appear partly related to screens “displacing caregiver talk, joint attention, peer play and hands-on exploration”.



Mum Jade Shields, 30, stops to chat as she walks her five-year-old son Leo Baiz home from school in ­Benwell.

She said: “Leo comes in from school and has his tea, then he’s allowed an hour or two of screen time. He has another half hour before he goes to sleep. I make sure that I know what he’s watching.

“There have been times when I’ve heard some swearing ­coming from his iPad and I’ve had to take it off him. I won’t let him watch anything inappropriate.”

Abel Lowe, five, is a fan of family-friendly YouTuber Jason Vlogs, who has more than 25million subscribers.



Abel’s mum Michelle, 34, has no problem with him watching safe content on devices.

She said: “Abel gets an hour a day of screen time as long as he’s been good at school and at home. I use it as a reward for good behaviour.

“I know what he’s watching and I can’t see anything harmful in that.”

And Michelle, who has three other kids, thinks it’s unfair for children to miss out.

She said: “We can’t expect them to see everyone else glued to their phones and not want to be part of that. You have to be realistic. If too much time on screens stops kids developing properly, there should be tighter controls on how old you have to be to have a phone.



“I’m really careful with my kids but maybe the Government should be doing more to keep kids safe.”

Lisa Frarey, 32, a singer-songwriter from Newcastle, is mum to Archie, four, and six-month-old Jack.

Archie gets to watch his favourite channels — including educational platform ABCmouse — on the family’s devices under a strict regime.

Lisa said: “We set a timer for half an hour at a time and when the timer goes off Archie knows that the screen has to go down.



“I don’t see a problem with him watching things on Disney and Netflix for short spells of time as long as I know what he’s watching.

“It gives me time to do what I need to do around the house and even to write some music, which is quite hard when you have two young kids.

“I don’t think kids should be left in front of a screen for hours at a time, but they are part of life now.”

Shanel Bruce, 33, is taking a break from her career in childcare while she brings up her first child. Aurora-Grace, who will be two next month, is allowed to use her mum’s phone.



Shanel said: “The only time I would give her my phone if we were out would be if we were in public and she had a meltdown through being over-tired.

“In the past few weeks we have definitely entered the terrible twos and sometimes there’s no pleasing her. In that circumstance I give her my phone to watch something that will soothe her — like Agent Binky, Bluey or Hey Duggee — and distract her from whatever is bothering her.

“But for the most part she loves her jigsaw puzzles and her toys.

“As someone who works in childcare I know how important it is for them to develop, and too much time in front of screens can damage that.”



Dame Andrea Leadsom, founder of 1001 Critical Days Foundation, worries about how damaging screen use can be for the youngest generation.

She said: “The clear evidence into the impact of screen use on babies is shocking — from developmental delay and a worrying association between high levels of screen use and behaviours sometimes observed in autistic children, to evidence of damage to the developing optic nerve. All governments need to do much more to help parents increase their own knowledge and give their baby the best start in life.”

At a playgroup in Westerhope, Newcastle, two-year-old Florence Beers is happily scooting around in a toy car. Her mum Katie Wynn, 37, said:

“Screen time for Florence is usually the TV but we will give her a phone or a tablet if we’re going on a long journey, because sometimes you just need to distract them.

“It is all about balance. My 11-year-old stepson likes to play Roblox a lot but he was five when the pandemic struck and young children at that time needed things to occupy them.



“Too much screen time can be damaging. I was really shocked to read a report about the show CoCo- melon, which is for young children but over-stimulates them by changing the scene less than every six seconds. Shows like that are designed to make viewing addictive.”

Rachel Vecht, founder of Educating Matters, which offers practical guidance on parenting, wants mums and dads to be aware of the impact of screen time on their children. She said: “Screens can’t adjust, mirror or respond in the way a human face does. All stimulus from the outside world adds to a baby’s neural network.

“High exposure to screens in babies is linked to delayed language, ­disrupted sleep and ­difficulties with attention and emotional ­regulation.”

Rachel added: “The fact that 85 per cent of parents in the 1001 Critical Days Foundation study say they had no guidance on screen time from health services is a systemic failure, not a parenting ­failure. Being a parent is the hardest job in the world with no training. It feels like there is so much conflicting guidance.

“Allowing young children to use screens has been normalised because we see it around us all the time.”



Dame Andrea believes it is time for change and parents must be better educated on phone use.

She added: “The case for action has never been stronger. All governments need to do much more to help parents increase their own knowledge and give their baby the best start in life.”

News.title: I confronted sick Don’t F**k With Cats killer in his lair before he sent me chilling email that would be his downfall
News.content:
TWISTED murderer Luka Magnotta boasted he was a “genius” who could not be caught after posting sick videos of cat killings – but his run in with The Sun led to his conviction for the gruesome crime he went on to commit.

The tale of the gay porn star’s horrific murder of Chinese student Jun Lin was made into an international Netflix sensation Don’t F*** With Cats – but that was only half the story.



Here, Sun journalist Alex West tells how Magnotta’s warped arrogance and a doorstep encounter at a London pub sealed his downfall.

IT began with a series of sick videos uploaded on the internet showing kittens being killed.

One was fed to a python and another suffocated in a plastic bag with a vacuum cleaner.

It ended with the horrific murder and dismemberment of a young student – his body parts sent in the post to politicians and schools in a case which rocked the world.



Luka Magnotta, a failed gay porn star from Canada, was being named as the source of the films by a group of internet sleuths – who would later go on to be the centre of the Netflix doc Don’t F*** With Cats.

In the middle of the night on December 8, 2011, we started getting emails to The Sun newsdesk from anonymous accounts saying that Magnotta was staying at a London pub, The Fusilier Inn in Wembley, where we would be able to confront him.

At 9am that morning, weirdo Magnotta turned up at The Sun offices in Wapping, east London.

He spoke to one of our reporters outside and demanded to know why he was being harassed by people contacting his hotel before disappearing.

When I arrived in the office the news desk told me to go to Wembley and speak to him as we believed he was the person behind the cat videos.



I quickly compiled a dossier of evidence – including pictures of a unique wolf design bedspread which appeared in his social media and one of the kitten films.

Photographer Simon Jones and I worked out that his room was around the back of the pub and climbed up an old iron fire escape and banged on the back door.

I thought that if he was behind the sick animal killings and boasting about them online, he would be a strange and dangerous individual.



I didn’t know then he would go on to be wanted for a gruesome sadistic murder and spark an international manhunt.

When he came to the door he was wearing a flat cap, leather jacket and tracksuit bottoms. He was wearing blue eye shadow and foundation make-up and he looked creepy.

His high pitch transatlantic voice was strained and out of place at the £40-a-night hotel, and he seemed anxious we were quizzing him.

Magnotta appeared from his online pictures to have all the trappings of wealth – his Facebook profile showed him at exotic locations in Paris, Moscow, Los Angeles and outside Buckingham Palace.

He had changed his name from Eric Clinton Newman to Luka Magnotta in an effort to disguise his small town rural Canadian upbringing and add mystique.



But the reality was grim.

His language was also dark – he claimed he did not want to be “hunted down and killed”.

I asked him about the videos but unusually he wasn’t shocked by the questions, instead he appeared to have rehearsed answers and denied everything.



He claimed he did not want to be interviewed and was a private person – yet he had posted swathes of pictures and information about himself online.

His story didn’t add up – he couldn’t give answers to questions, and he was clearly fully aware of everything I was talking about.

After 20 minutes of interrogation I elicited a confession of sorts. I asked if he had received death threats for the videos he posted online of him killing the kittens, he replied yes.

When I asked if then he had killed the kittens, he said I was twisting his words.

When pointed to the pictures of him posing on the bedspread with the kittens – the same bedspread seen in the killing video – he changed his tune and said his picture had been digitally altered.



After a while I gave up the questioning and we left.

We stayed outside and kept an eye on his room while I typed up my interview.

A few hours later we watched as plain clothed police officers arrived and escorted him from the hotel.



The hotel owner had complained after receiving calls about him and wanted him to leave. We called the Met Police and said we had this information about Magnotta – but they said there was no real crime that they could investigate.

Two days later the news desk received a really dark email to the office from someone who could only be Magnotta.

It detailed horrific violent sex acts he planned to do.

It also boasted that he could not be caught and that the next time it would not be animals that he would kill.

In one line it paraphrased a quote from Basic Instinct saying: “You see, killing is different than smoking…with smoking you can actually quit.”



The message was sent using the alias John Kilbride, one of the child victims of the Moors Murderers Ian Brady and Myra Hindley.

In one of the videos that he posted of the cat killing, Magnotta is playing the song The Little Drummer Boy in the background.

The Little Drummer Boy was also being played in the background on a tape recorded by Ian Brady when he killed Leslie Ann Downey.

In his dark words he boasted of his “genius” at not being caught.



The letter said: “I have to say goodbye for now, but don’t worry. In the near future, you’ll be hearing from me again.

“This time, however, the victims won’t be small animals.

“I will, however, send you a copy of the new video I’m going to be making. You see, killing is different than smoking. With smoking, you can actually quit.

“Once you kill and taste blood, it’s impossible to stop.

“The urge is just too strong not to continue. The fun part of all this is watching millions of people get angry and frustrated because they can’t catch me.



“That’s why I love this. I love the risk factor. It’s so fun watching people work so hard, gathering all the evidence, then not being able to name me or catch me.

“You see, I always win. I always hold the trump card. And I’ll continue to make more movies. London is wonderful because all the people are so stupid.

“So, I have to disappear for a while, you know, until people quit bothering me. But next time you hear from me, it will be in a movie I am producing, that will have some humans in it, not just pussys.

“The things I have seen and the things I have done, you can only imagine.

“Getting away with all this, now that’s genius.”



It was like a confession note written in advance where he set out what he would go on to do.

The email became key evidence in his murder trial to prove that it was premeditated.

I reported the letter to the press bureau – the communication arm of the Met Police who said I should take it in and speak to an officer about it.



The following day, I went to Limehouse Police Station and gave a full statement to a detective.

We passed over the email and the other evidence.

But the police came back and said there was nothing they could do about it.

The email itself appeared to have been sent from the Netherlands.

Magnotta had either used a VPN or had just moved to Holland where he sent the email.

The videos of the cat killings were posted in North America.



As a result the Met said it was out of their jurisdiction and they couldn’t do anymore and recorded it as a “malicious communication”.

The sense that Magnotta had just disappeared was frustrating.

But his sick bragging would ultimately come back to haunt him as it proved premeditation for his murder.

Months passed and I thought little more about it and got back to work on other stories.

Then in May 2012 I was at home in West London and got a call from the newsdesk saying Magnotta was wanted by police for horrifically killing and chopping up Chinese student Jun Lin in Canada.



He had brought this young man back to his apartment in Montreal and drugged him.

Whilst unconscious he stabbed him with a screwdriver painted silver to resemble an ice pick and then chopped his head off and chopped off his limbs.

He filmed the mutilation and posted it online under the name 1 Lunatic 1 Icepick.



It was a hideous homage to the Basic Instinct movie, in which Sharon Stone’s character kills her lover with an ice pick while straddling him.

It showed him performing sick sex acts with the dismembered body.

He then sent body parts including a hand and foot to politicians and schools across Canada.

Jun’s head was found discarded by a nearby lake.

Six months after we met him at that London pub, he had acted out what he had threatened to do in the email he sent us.



Following his gruesome crime Magnotta went on the run in Europe and an international manhunt was launched.

I was warned there was a chance he could be coming to London. But days later he was arrested in Berlin in an internet café where he was googling his own crime.

A year later on March 11, 2013, Magnotta was due to appear for a preliminary hearing in Montreal.

I was dispatched by the news desk to go out and cover the hearing.

When I arrived at the courthouse I was informed by the police that they wanted me to give evidence in the case.



Magnotta was brought into court by the custody officer.

He was bent over and sullen, his eyes sunken and expressionless.

He sat disengaged in the dock as the charges were read out against him.

The judge asked me if I knew Luka Magnotta and if I recognised him in court. I was asked to point him out in front of the judge, legal teams and the other press.

Magnotta did not lift his eyes as I pointed in his direction and said: “That’s him.”



He was a completely different vision to the cocky but weird man I had seen at the hotel months earlier.

I had surreptitiously recorded the almost 30 minute exchange and the audio tape was played in Magnotta’s trial – the only time the jury heard the beast speak.

The email he sent afterwards became key evidence that the murder was premeditated.

I was cross-examined by Magnotta’s lawyer who tried to suggest this man was not guilty of murder because of mental illness.

But the jury saw through that veil of lies and convicted him correctly of first degree murder.



The Sun’s part in the twisted saga helped nail the killer.

After Magnotta was convicted, prosecutor Louis Bouthillier called the email “a very important part of our case”.

Magnotta will rot behind bars for the rest of his life – condemned by his own warped arrogance.

News.title: Army unveils design for new uncrewed helicopter drone that will protect Appache gunships from attack by hostile forces
News.content:
PLANS for drone helicopters to protect manned Apache gunships have been revealed by the Army.

The so-called robo-choppers will fly in swarms and will be loaded with sensors and weapons to detect and destroy hostile forces before they can threaten pilots’ lives.





Concept art of the BAE Systems pilotless tech has been released.

The firm will split £10million with three other companies to develop the drones as part of Project Nyx.

The MoD said the aircraft will be fully autonomous and Apache pilots “will benefit from the information they’re providing, without needing to control them directly”.

But decisions to unleash weapons “will continue to be made by a human,” the MoD insisted.

Other firms involved in development include the UK divisions of French giant Thales, US firm Anduril and Portuguese company Tekever.

Defence Minister Luke Pollard said the robo-chopper programme would give troops an “unbeatable advantage on the battlefield”.

He said: “This is British ingenuity at its best – cutting-edge drones working alongside Apache helicopters to give our soldiers an unbeatable advantage on the battlefield.

“The UK isn’t just keeping up with the future of warfare, we’re driving it.”



It comes after Army chief General Sir Roly Walker was overruled by ministers over a £1billion order for 23 new choppers, which he said were a lesser priority to drones.

The first aircraft from Project Nyx is expected to enter service in 2030.

News.title: It’s scary knowing he’s still out there, says waitress who was knocked out by violent migrant before he went on the run
News.content:
A YOUNG waitress knocked unconscious by a violent asylum seeker who then went on the run said yesterday: “It’s scary knowing he’s still out there.”

Cleo Lake, 21, suffered a broken nose when she was punched by coward Abdoela Berhan after she rejected his advances outside a club.





Shocking footage showed the Eritrean flooring Cleo in Bournemouth and running off, leaving her helpless in December 2024.

Berhan, 35, who was living at taxpayers’ expense in the town’s Britannia Hotel, was arrested later but claimed he acted in self-defence.

We revealed in August last year that it is one of three prime hotels near the town’s beach used to house migrants, angering tourists and locals.

Berhan was found guilty of assault in his absence after dodging court — just a week after he was convicted of attacking a Subway worker in another incident.

He was also found guilty of criminal damage to a police cell in a third trial in his absence.

Despite there being three warrants out for his arrest, Berhan remains at large, with police saying only that “enquiries are ongoing”.

Cleo said: “It’s frustrating knowing he still hasn’t been picked up. It’s scary knowing he’s probably still out there, maybe still in the area.

“I know how slow the police are with things — it doesn’t feel like they are trying very hard.”



Her mum, Helen O’Brien, who saw the footage of the attack in court, said: “It was shocking and upsetting.

“Cleo had told me about what happened but watching a video of a grown man hurting your child is devastating. I’m just grateful she wasn’t hurt more.

“I feel he’s never going to be found. He’s roaming around somewhere.



“He’s violent and isn’t going to stop because he’s not had any consequences for what he’s done.

“I’m angry there’s no background checks on people like this coming into our country.

“We all have to have passports, National Insurance, driving licences to say who we are and they have nothing.

“We’ve no idea what he’s capable of. It’s frightening.”

Berhan had sat next to Cleo as she and two friends sat outside a club and tried to put his arm around one of them after they left. Cleo told him to “f**k off” and pushed him away.



Berhan aimed a kick at her and she retaliated with a kick, at which point he punched her and fled.

Cleo told Poole JPs of the effect the assault had on her. She said: “After, I didn’t go out for a while. I got quite bad anxiety around men.

“Even now, a year and a half later, I won’t go clubbing unless there’s a lot of us or someone’s boyfriend is there, for protection.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Judge Orla Austin said she was satisfied of Berhan’s guilt and issued an arrest warrant.

She said: “Prison is very much in the forefront of my mind”.

News.title: Labour mob won’t last 3 years… we’ll win Election within 12 months, says Nigel Farage as he reveals thoughts on being PM
News.content:
“THIS mob won’t last three years” chortles Nigel Farage in his first major interview since painting the map of Britain turquoise at last week’s local elections.

After cutting through Labour and Tory-held town halls across the land like butter, the Reform boss is like the cat that’s got the cream as he predicts a General Election victory in under 12 months.





Asked how he can be so sure, he warns we are on the cusp of a major economic downturn sweeping what’s left of this Labour government out of office — and some “tough love” and leadership will be needed to fix it.

He said: “I based that on what Labour would do to business confidence, to private sector investment, to employment — and I think the bond markets already are giving us a message.”

And as the Manchester mayor makes his own play for No10, Farage has a new target in his sights: “It’s amazing, isn’t it? I mean, Andy Burnham says ‘don’t worry about the bond markets. Bond markets will come to you. It will all be fine you know’.

“Well, it won’t be. So, no, I think there is a bad time coming economically for the UK, but it’s not very far away.”

But the smile soon drops when asked how he feels about the prospect of sitting in No10 this time next year as Prime Minister.

“It’s slightly daunting”, he admits, “I’d be a fool not to say that, but I still, in my own mind, see it as being some way off.”

He insists Reform is stepping up a gear to prepare for government after gaining more than 1,400 councillors last week and taking control of a dozen new councils.

But is he ready? “We’ve been a work in progress. We’ve come an astonishing way in one year and ten months. An astonishing way in that short period of time. I’d say we’re now two-thirds ready.”



Just don’t call it a one-man band any more. Farage insists that notion is “utter bilge” and the party would survive even if its superstar leader had the misfortune of falling under a bus.

“This really hacks me off. I mean, come on. This one-man band thing.

“You know, in the last four months I’ve appointed a leader in Scotland, I’ve appointed a leader in Wales.



“I’ve appointed four major shadow cabinet positions. I’ve appointed a head of policy for the party, a head of preparing for government for the party.

“I keep appointing people and they keep going on media all the time. They keep appearing in public all the time. And I’m still told it’s a one-man band.”

Despite some high-profile departures from his operation — like the ex-Reform MP Rupert Lowe — Mr Farage insists he is ready to share the load in power and play well with others.

“Most people in this building we’re sitting in now, my inner team, and you know them all, have been with me for over a decade.

“There are people in this building who have been with me for over 25 years. I maintain long-term work relationships with most people that ever crossed my path.



“Even all my staff who worked for me in the ’90s, 30 years ago in the City, are all still personal friends.”

“I don’t fall out with people”, he insists, before adding with a hint of menace: “What happens in politics is you get people who think they’re much cleverer than you and that they got elected to the European Parliament because of who they were.

“And they all get a bit too big for their boots.



“They decide to take me on and then — maybe I’m not quite as friendly then.” Yet he says: “I’m perfectly relaxed about people disagreeing with me. Just don’t do it in public.

“You can come into my office, you can call me any words you like. I don’t mind one little bit.

“You can scream and shout at me, I don’t mind one little bit.”

But as he seeks to build a team to win a General Election, Mr Farage says he is in pole position, despite only a third of voters backing his party.

“I think this political movement has caught the mood,” he said. “It’s crossed the British class system in a way no party’s ever done before. It’s crossing geographies, unlike any other party at the moment.



NO TO No10 MOVE By Harry Cole MR Farage may not live at 10 ­Downing Street if he becomes PM. Asked if he was ready to move into Britain’s most famous address, the Reform chief said he “shouldn’t think” he would bother. PMs have traditionally lived in the flats above, but some disliked the intense atmosphere. As for the next election, Farage said he was unlikely to face unpopular Keir Starmer. He dismissed potential successors Andy Burnham and Wes Streeting as lightweights, but praised “real” Angela Rayner. On going up against any of them in a TV debate, he quipped: “It’d be a lot more fun with Angie.”

“We’re winning seats in the valleys of Wales to the North East of Scotland.

“You know, we’re literally across the whole country. We’re competitive everywhere, apart from the odd inner London borough.”

But like it was for his pal, US President Donald Trump, Mr Farage fears the next 12 months will see the gloves come off as the old parties and establishment go into a tailspin to try to stop him crossing the threshold of No10.

He says he has “no choice” but to hunker down for the fight, adding: “I’ve had years of it already. They will always find something to attack me on.”



But he insists his message is the one resonating with the public, saying: “The last poll I saw said that 74 per cent of the population agree Britain is broken.

“And if you accept something’s broken, then you realise only radical change, that’s all you can do to change things.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Kemi says Britain’s not broken. Great. Keir says Britain’s not broken. Fine. I believe Britain is broken at every level. And I know most of the electorate say that.

“So is this a country ready for some radical change and frankly for some quite tough medicine in some areas?”

News.title: One of UK’s ‘most wanted’ men Simon Dutton, 49, arrested near Benidorm for drug trafficking
News.content:
ONE of Britain’s most wanted fugitives has been arrested by Spanish cops near Benidorm after being on the run for months.

Simon Dutton, 49, was cuffed following a stunning police raid – and has now been charged been drug trafficking and document forgery.





The high-stakes arrest is understood to have happened in La Nucia in the early hours of Thursday morning.

Local cops only went public with it later in the day after the National Crime Agency unveiled the latest Operation Captura wanted list in Alicante.

Before his arrest on Thursday, he had been wanted for a re-call to prison.

The Costa Blanca arrest was filmed in dramatic footage – with Dutton seen swarmed by heavily armed cops in a white villa.



Storming the property, they shouted in English: “Police, police.”

They raided the home with sniffer dogs and were pictured counting out large wads of cash in the aftermath.



The arrest cane just hours after the launch of a new campaign aiming to hunt down 12 fugitives believed to be hiding on the Costas.

Spanish police said: “The Civil Guard in Alicante has arrested one of the fugitives included in the UK-led international search operation against offenders linked to organised crime, coinciding with the presentation of the latest ‘Most Wanted’ campaign.

“The arrest has been carried out within the framework of an operation conducted in Benidorm and La Nucia against a network linked to drug trafficking and forgery, in which three other people have been arrested.”



They added: “The investigation began in November 2025 following a tip-off from the manager of a Benidorm courier firm where a suitcase containing 16 kilos of cannabis resin had been located which was due to be sent to the UK.

“Initial inquiries led to the identification of a woman who organised the delivery using false documentation.

“Investigators discovered she went to the establishment with another person and had logistical support from another two men who transported the suitcase.

“As the investigation advanced officers managed to identify those involved and confirm one was a person on the UK Most Wanted list for crimes relating to drug trafficking who an International Arrest Warrant had been issued for at the end of last year.”

The Manchester fugitive is set to face a national court after being charged with drug trafficking and document forgery.



He was cuffed alongside two other suspects, while a fourth woman was arrested in Costa Blanca.

Police seized various narcotics, about £3,000 in cash, false documents and two cars.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Dutton, who has the name “Rachel” tattooed on his left arm, was sentenced to 14 years in prison in September 2016 for organising large-scale importations of cocaine.

One police operation linked to him uncovered 10.5kg of drugs with a street value of £1.5million.

News.title: Woman suffers brain injuries after falling from balcony to escape 'gang rape'
News.content:
Woman suffers brain injuries after falling from balcony to escape 'gang rape'

The victim is said to have fallen from the second floor of an apartment building in Germany and suffered severe injuries while allegedly trying to flee a group of five men

A young woman has reportedly suffered catastrophic brain injuries after falling from a balcony while allegedly trying to escape being raped by a group of men.

‌



The victim is said to have fallen from the second floor of an apartment building in Germany while trying to flee the five unidentified suspects, according to Bild. Local police have confirmed an investigation is underway.

‌



Police, paramedics and the fire department raced to the building on Senftenberger Straße at 3:15am on Tuesday.

‌



The woman had reportedly been helped back inside her apartment by the five men.

View 2 Images Police have confirmed an investigation is underway (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Due to the severity of her injuries, an emergency physician vehicle was deployed before the woman was rushed to hospital.

Doctors said the victim had suffered traumatic brain injuries. She is currently receiving treatment.

Police sources confirmed to Bild that a possible sexual offence had occurred inside the apartment and was being investigated.

Article continues below

Officers have carried out searches at the property as part of their investigation.,

Forensic inspectors collected samples from the scene on Wednesday, but police have not ruled out the possibility that the suspected perpetrators could have made attempts to destroy existing evidence.

News.title: 'Most wanted' British fugitive with distinctive tattoo arrested near Benidorm
News.content:
'Most wanted' British fugitive with distinctive tattoo arrested near Benidorm

Simon Dutton - one of Britain’s most wanted fugitives - has been arrested near Benidorm in Spain just hours after he was named by the NCA in a list of most wanted men

View Image Simon Dutton (Image: NCA)

Spanish police have arrested a British fugitive just hours after he was named in a list of 12 "most wanted" men believed to be hiding in Spain.

‌



Simon Dutton, 49, was held in La Nucia just north of Benidorm today. The arrest is understood to have happened in the early hours of this morning, although cops only went public with it late tonight after the National Crime Agency (NCA) unveiled the latest Operation Captura wanted list.

‌



Dutton, from Bolton, "organised the importation of cocaine from Spain to the UK, with one police interception uncovering 10.5kg with a street value of £1.5 million", the NCA said.

‌



Dutton, who the NCA said has the name ‘Rachel’ tattooed on his left arm as well as "scars on his chin, left hand and right leg", was arrested in Spain as part of an investigation into alleged drug trafficking and document forgery. Three other people were arrested.

The Civil Guard released footage showing heavily-armed officers surrounding a whitewashed villa before forcing entry as they shouted in English: "Police, police."

A spokesman for the Civil Guard, which didn’t officially name Dutton, said tonight: “The Civil Guard in Alicante has arrested one of the fugitives included in the UK-led international search operation against offenders linked to organised crime, coinciding with the presentation of the latest ‘Most Wanted’ campaign.

‌



“The arrest has been carried out within the framework of an operation conducted in Benidorm and La Nucia against a network linked to drug trafficking and forgery, in which three other people have been arrested.

“The investigation began in November 2025 following a tip-off from the manager of a Benidorm courier firm where a suitcase containing 16 kilos of cannabis resin had been located which was due to be sent to the UK.

“Initial inquiries led to the identification of a woman who organised the delivery using false documentation.

‌



“Investigators discovered she went to the establishment with another person and had logistical support from another two men who transported the suitcase.

“As the investigation advanced officers managed to identify those involved and confirm one was a person on the UK Most Wanted list for crimes relating to drug trafficking who an International Arrest Warrant had been issued for at the end of last year.”

It came following the NCA's publication of the latest list of fugitives - including Dutton - marking the 20th anniversary of Operation Captura - a multi-agency campaign which has seen 98 fugitives apprehended out of 111 publicised.

Article continues below

All men featured in this year’s campaign are believed to have links to Spain including areas such as Tenerife, Marbella, Alicante, and Malaga.

News.title: Will Eid Al-Adha 2026 moon be seen in UK? Dates Dhul Hijjah may start revealed
News.content:
Will Eid Al-Adha 2026 moon be seen in UK? Dates Dhul Hijjah may start revealed

Muslims across the UK await Saudi Arabia's Eid Al-Adha 2026 moon sighting announcement as experts predict exactly when the celebrations could begin later this month

View 4 Images Saudi Arabia is expected to carry out the official moon sighting for Dhul Hijjah (file image) (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Muslims around the world are preparing for the Eid Al-Adha 2026 moon sighting, with astronomers predicting the Dhul Hijjah crescent could be visible in Saudi Arabia, the UAE and parts of the UK later this month.

‌



The crescent moon, which marks the start of the Islamic month, could be visible on the evening of May 17, astronomers say, though the exact date will depend on confirmed sightings. If the moon is seen, Dhul Hijjah - the final month of the Islamic calendar - would begin on May 18, placing Eid Al-Adha on or around May 27.

‌



Eid al-Adha is one of the most important festivals in Islam and is usually celebrated over three days.

‌



Muslims typically attend special prayers, spend time with family and friends, share meals and give to charity, while many also mark the occasion with the ritual sacrifice of an animal, with meat often distributed to those in need.

View 4 Images Saudi moon sighting committees will look for the crescent shortly after sunset (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Eid holiday rules around taking time off work for Eid ul Adha and Eid ul Fitr READ MORE :

When will Dhul Hijjah moon be visible in Saudi Arabia?

Saudi Arabia is expected to carry out the official moon sighting for Dhul Hijjah on the evening of May 17, 2026.

‌



The Kingdom's moon sighting committees will look for the crescent shortly after sunset, with astronomers suggesting viewing conditions could be favourable in parts of the Middle East.

If the crescent is confirmed, May 18 would become the first day of Dhul Hijjah. Eid Al-Adha takes place on the 10th day of that month, so would likely begin on May 27.

If the moon is not sighted, the Islamic month of Dhul Qa'dah would complete 30 days, pushing Eid back by one day.

‌



View 4 Images Eid Al-Adha is expected to begin in late May (Image: Martin O'Callaghan)

Could the Eid Al-Adha 2026 moon be seen in the UK?

Some Muslims in the UK follow moon sightings announced by Saudi Arabia, while others might rely on local sightings.

Weather conditions can affect whether the crescent is seen in Britain, meaning communities can sometimes begin Islamic months on different dates.

‌



Experts say the crescent moon may be difficult to spot with the naked eye in parts of the UK on May 17, but telescopes and clear skies may improve visibility.

Mosques and Islamic organisations across Britain are expected to issue guidance closer to the expected sighting date.

View 4 Images Muslim countries may announce the start of Dhu al-Hijjah on different days (Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)

Article continues below

Why do Eid dates differ around the world?

Eid dates can vary because different countries and Islamic authorities use different methods to determine the start of the lunar month.

Some rely strictly on physical moon sightings, while others use astronomical calculations to predict when the crescent should be visible.

This means Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Pakistan, Morocco and the UK can sometimes announce the beginning of Dhu al-Hijjah on different days.

News.title: Snooker pro's mum to be reported to authorities after bitter legal battle over family home
News.content:
Snooker pro's mum to be reported to authorities after bitter legal battle over family home

The referral was revealed after world No43 Matthew Selt was taken to court by Susan Hickenbotham in a row over the family home

View 5 Images Matthew Selt was taken to court by his mum Susan Hickenbotham (Image: Supplied by Champion News)

A snooker pro's mum will be referred to the authorities for alleged housing benefits fraud after a bitter legal battle over a £620,000 family house.

Susan Hickenbotham claimed her son Matthew Selt, the world No43, his sisters Claire Noble and Charlotte Hamblin ganged up and demanded she sign the family home over to them, reducing her to tears. Hickenbotham, who has been claiming social security and housing benefits since 1992, claimed ownership of the house in Romford, where she has lived since 1998, and which is now worth around £620,000.

Hickenbotham was served an eviction notice by her daughter Claire Noble in 2024. She claimed she bought the property from her ex-husband Michael David Selt for £75,000, as a gesture of goodwill after they split up. The mum-of-three claimed she put £7,500 towards the mortgage in 2000 and bought the house outright in 2011 after she was left some money by her father.

View 5 Images Susan Hickenbotham is the mum of snooker player Matthew Selt, ranked 43 in the world (Image: Champion News)

She claimed this money was given to Noble to put towards the house, but Noble kept it for herself. Hickenbotham's lawyer has claimed her children created a 'sham tenancy', listing Noble as the owner and her mother as the tenant so she could claim housing benefit. Selt, 41, said he didn't remember the details of the property being acquired in 2000 or the deed signing in 2019.

Judge Simon Monty KC on Thursday warned the family the case could end in "mutually assured destruction." In his judgement, he said Hickenbotham's account of how she raised £7,500 to put towards the house was "unconvincing." He said Hickenbotham did pay Claire £7,500 in cash to Ms Noble but it was to be used towards renovations rather than being a deposit.

The judge said: "None of Susan, Claire or Charlotte come out of this well and I did not think that any of them were convincing witnesses. I approach their evidence, all of it, with considerable caution." The judge decided Hickenbotham was lying about being forced to sign a deed.

View 5 Images Hickenbotham claimed her kids forced her to sign over the deeds to the family home (Image: Supplied by Champion News)

He said: "In my view, there was a meeting, which was probably on 6 June 2019, at the property, attended by Susan and the three children. There was no draft deed produced at the meeting, and there was no shouting by the children. Claire went through the proposed deed, and whilst she and her siblings were very keen that Susan should sign it, there was at that time no document to be signed and nothing was signed at that meeting.

"I do not accept Susan's version of events- I accept what Claire, Matthew and Charlotte say about the meeting. None of the children recall Mark being there. He was not. I do not accept anything Susan says about the shouting or the tears or her being distressed and upset. I regret to have concluded that Susan has made all of this up."

The judge dismissed Hickenbotham's claim but said she did contribute £7,500 to the purchase. He also concluded that Hickenbotham had given Noble £96,000 which she had got to her father in order to pay off her mortgage but that Ms Noble did not put it into the mortgage. The judge said the tenancy document was a 'sham' by Noble and Hickenbotham to deceive the local authority.

View 5 Images Matthew made his first 147 of his 24-year career at the BetVictor Championship League in January (Image: Getty Images)

He said: "Susan, with the assistance of Claire, has perpetrated what appears to have been a housing benefits fraud between 2000 and 2019 by setting up a false tenancy agreement naming as the tenant the true owner of the property knowingly in order to receive housing benefit which was used to pay the mortgage. I do not think Charlotte was involved. Matthew was not involved.

"Although Susan had a 10 per cent share in the property, the deed was freely entered into. By the deed, Susan declared that she had no interest in the property. The claim is dismissed. I intend to report Susan and Claire to the appropriate authorities in relation to the apparent benefits fraud. This is a very sorry, and I have to say, entirely predictable, end to these unhappy proceedings."

Tom Russell, KC, representing his mum, earlier said the sportsman gave "no significant detail" during his evidence. He said: "I wonder if this is an effect of his profession, being in the public eye, which is to deny everything. It was like a no comment interview, he didn't recognise any documentation, he did not recognise any facts of the case supported by documentation," he said.

He said Selt could not remember details of his eldest son's first birthday party, at which Mr Selt and his siblings say the deed was signed by their mother in 2019. Judge Monty had said Selt was not as involved in the case as his mother and sisters. He said: "He's not really at the centre of all of this, he's the most distant."

View 5 Images Matthew Selt was not involved in the fraud (Image: PA)

Hamblin, who represented herself and her siblings, told the court: "The claimant has shown she can be violent to both the public and her family. Hamblin said there were "huge evidential gaps" in her mother's case, and that she had been happy with the arrangement on the house for years before bringing the lawsuit.

Article continues below

She said for years there was "no mention of the deed, no mention of the tears, and no mention of the duress." She added: "It is only when the claimant's relationship with the first defendant [her eldest daughter Ms Noble] failed, and she was asked to leave because of her own evidenced conduct. The claimant agreed under oath her divorce was toxic. "What is more likely, that the father wanted his children to have the property, or he wanted to give it to his ex-wife?"

Hamblin said an email from her dad was shown to the court "confirming he did not want the property to go to his ex wife," adding: "He is either not being truthful in court to benefit herself financially, or she has been lying to the benefits system for many years both are acts of dishonesty."

Matthew made his first 147 of his 24-year career at the BetVictor Championship League in January. Last year he was removed from his position as vice-chairman of the World Professional Billiards and Snooker Association (WPBSA) players' association for 'rude and aggressive' behaviour at the 2024 Saudi Arabia Masters.

News.title: Keir Starmer won't block Andy Burnham's Westminster comeback as grip on power weakens
News.content:
Keir Starmer won't block Andy Burnham's Westminster comeback as grip on power weakens

Keir Starmer’s grip on power appears more perilous after Andy Burnham unveiled a dramatic route back to Parliament and Wes Streeting quit the government

View 4 Images Keir Starmer's grip on power weakened after a dramatic day in Westminster (Image: POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

Keir Starmer’s grip on power appears more perilous after Andy Burnham unveiled a dramatic route back to Parliament and Wes Streeting quit the government.

‌



The Greater Manchester Mayor confirmed he would seek a return after the Labour MP for Makerfield, Josh Simons, resigned his seat and triggered a by-election. Mr Burnham said: “I grew up in this area and have lived here for 25 years. I care deeply about it and its people. I know they have been let down by national politics.” He added he wanted to return to Westminster to “bring the change we have brought to Greater Manchester to the whole of the UK and make politics work properly for people”.

‌



Dubbed the King of the North, Mr Burnham must now win approval of Labour’s governing body to allow him to defend the party’s majority of just over 5,000 votes and take the fight to Nigel Farage’s Reform UK.

‌



In February, Mr Starmer and members of the National Executive Committee (NEC) blocked the Greater Manchester Mayor’s return to Parliament by 8-1. But with the Prime Minister’s authority now in tatters after a brutal week of civil war at the top of Labour’s ranks, it is understood he will not seek to lock Mr Burnham a second time.

View 4 Images Wes Streeting resigned as Health Secretary and accused Keir Starmer of offering a 'vacuum' instead of a vision (Image: POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

An ally of the Prime Minister said: “Keir is focused on bringing the party together so it can tackle the issues facing working families.”

‌



One Labour MP told The Mirror: “Andy Burnham is our best chance of stopping Reform. Most people now recognise that and that’s why Streeting doesn’t have the numbers."

But Cabinet minister Steve Reed hit back, saying: "I’m sorry Josh has taken this decision. If anyone thinks there is a caped superhero that is coming our way with all the answers they have another thing coming."

Mr Burnham’s dramatic announcement came as Mr Streeting also quit as Health Secretary and called on Mr Starmer to resign. But he stopped short of triggering a leadership contest as had been expected. In a scathing resignation letter, the Labour heavyweight said it was clear the Prime Minister will not lead the party into the next general election. “Where we need vision, we have a vacuum,” he said. “Where we need direction, we have drift”

‌



He said a contest to replace the PM should “be broad” with the “best possible field of candidates”, adding: “I support that approach and I hope that you will facilitate this.” His failure to fire the starting gun on a leadership challenge raised speculation the former Cabinet minister had failed to secure the required 81 MPs’ nominations - 20% of the Parliamentary Labour Party - required to do so.

Andy Burnham confirms bid for return to Parliament but major hurdles remain READ MORE :

All the Labour MPs calling for Keir Starmer to quit - find out if your MP is one of them READ MORE :

View 4 Images Andy Burnham (above) said he would try to stand in a by-election in the North West to become an MP - after Labour MP Josh Simons stood down (Image: Getty Images)

But allies of Mr Streeting were adamant on Thursday he had sufficient support. In his resignation letter, Mr Streeting instead suggested the Prime Minister should first set out a timetable for his departure. He said: “It is now clear that you will not lead the Labour Party into the next general election and that Labour MPs and Labour Unions want the debate about what comes next to be a battle of ideas, not of personalities or petty factionalism.

‌



"It needs to be broad, and it needs the best possible field of candidates. I support that approach and I hope that you will facilitate this."

In a letter responding, Mr Starmer, who has previously vowed to fight any leadership challenge, said: “I am very sorry that you have stepped down from government. We have worked together for many years and I want to thank you for all your hard work in helping to get us back into government and for all that you have achieved as Health Secretary.”

A Labour MP supportive of Mr Streeting told The Mirror: “Keir needs to accept reality and set out a timetable for his departure. Wes did the principled thing and resigned and called for a full and proper contest.”

‌



But Mr Streeting’s path to power appeared to narrow as Angela Rayner also revealed she had been cleared of deliberate wrongdoing by HMRC over her tax affairs. It opens the door for her to launch her own bid for Downing Street if the contest is triggered. Ms Rayner, who was forced to resign as Deputy Prime Minister in September last year over the issue, has now settled a £40,000 payment in unpaid stamp duty. She indicated she may enter any Labour leadership contest that is triggered saying she wanted to “play my part”.

View 4 Images Angela Rayner revealed she had been cleared of deliberate wrongdoing by HMRC over her tax affairs (Image: AP Photo/Kirsty Wigglesworth)

But the former Cabinet minister ruled out launching a coup against the PM herself, telling the Guardian: “I’ve made it clear that I wasn’t going to trigger the prime minister - and that I want to see change. I want to see actions, not just words.”

‌



Ms Rayner also denied making any deals with Mr Burnham, who was spotted at the former Cabinet minister’s Ashton-under-Lyne home in Greater Manchester last month.

During a day of high-drama at Westminster, there were also reports that the armed forces minister Al Carns could throw his hat into the ring of any contest despite only entering the Commons two years ago.

In a speech on Friday morning, Deputy Labour leader Lucy Powell is expected to make a plea for unity after the mud-slinging and in-fighting in the party’s ranks in recent days.

‌



She will tell the Fire Brigades’ Union conference: “The election results last week were deeply painful and difficult for our Party, and the aftermath has been unedifying for us all too. We don’t do hostile take-overs in Labour for a reason. Keir is the Leader, and I warned against bloody internal battles reflecting badly.

“If we think we don’t have further to fall, that’s a mistake, we can. We must come back together as one team to take the fight to Farage and show that mainstream progressive politics can bring about the change people are crying out for. That also means doing politics differently. Ending briefing wars, ending factionalism, and representing all our traditions with our strongest team on the pitch - being one Labour team.

“Andy Burnham, Wes Streeting and Angela Rayner should all be key players in our team. Andy wants to come back to Parliament - I’ve always supported his desire to do so, and I support that again. As Deputy Leader, I am confident he would have the support of the vast majority of the Party and movement in doing so.”

Article continues below

Meanwhile, Chancellor Rachel Reeves warned colleagues not to put the economy “at risk” by “plunging the country into chaos” after figures showed gross domestic product grew in the first three months of the year. She said: “We shouldn't put that at risk by plunging the country in chaos at a time when there is conflict in the world."

News.title: Hope beats hate as simple acts of kindness change lives across UK
News.content:
There’s a phrase that sums up A Million Acts of Hope, and it belongs to Mary Hustler, a stalwart at the Sandale Community Hub on the Buttershaw Estate in Bradford. “If you’ve got the time,” the 81-year-old Bradfordian says, "turn up and get buttering!” It could be a slogan for the Buttershaw itself, a sprawling 1940s-60s council estate immortalised in the film Rita, Sue and Bob Too. But Mary, a former care worker and great-grandmother, is talking about a community food scheme that can involve buttering 400 slices of bread a day in the school holidays.

“No-one needs to go without here, we’ll make sure of it,” Mary says, cheerfully. “We laugh together and we cry together, but we are together.” Mary is part of the brilliantly-named group, ’Recycled Teenagers’ who meet at the Sandale, and include veteran members Lillian, 102 and Cynthia, 97.

“Community is very strong here,” says fellow Recycled Teenager, Kath Johnson, 71. “It’s who we are. Times are hard – this cost of living isn’t going away, this area can get talked down, but we look after each other.”

View 6 Images Kath Johnson, Anne Newsome and Mary Hustler from 'Recycled Teenagers’ at Sandale Community Hub (Image: Andy Stenning/Daily Mirror)

‌



A Million Acts of Hope is the broadest and deepest coalition of charities, community groups and faith organisations this decade. Two months after launching in the Mirror, this weekend Britain will celebrate a million moments of kindness, solidarity and connection, the length and breadth of the country.

A letter signed by over 70,000 people – including some very well known names, 239 charity partners and countless community groups – ran in Wednesday's Mirror. “To the people who give up evenings and weekend lie-ins,” the letter said. “Who pour tea, answer phones, raise funds, make lunches… To the people that get people talking – across divides and in tricky times. We thank you.

“Thank you for rolling up your sleeves. For not giving up… You are the beating hearts of our villages, towns and cities. And because hate can seem louder than hope these days, we have never needed you more. Luckily there are loads of you – quietly helping, shouldering burdens, building bridges. Please know there are even more of us, truly grateful for your graft, who also believe there is more that connects us than divides us.”

This week, we’ve been on tour across the country speaking to some of these tea-pourers and bridge-builders across different generations and different backgrounds. And wherever we have looked – whether in Bradford or Birmingham, Hertfordshire, Cardiff or Greater Manchester – we have found the most extraordinary people doing hopeful things.

‌



View 6 Images Founder Naima Ali at Uplift's coffee morning in Birmingham. (Image: Andy Stenning/Daily Mirror)

In Birmingham’s Small Heath, we met Naima Ali, a single mum-of-two, who grew up in Kenya. One morning when Naima was dropping her son to school, she noticed a mother at reception struggling to understand that her son needed his swimming kit. Naima stepped in to help. But as the weeks went on, she saw other mums with very little English struggling too. Stopping to chat to them after drop off, she walked with them to Aldi, bought coffee and then sat with them in a bus stop googling local colleges.

“We walked to Stonehall Adult Education, then to Sparkhill the same day,” she says. “Within four weeks, they were all enrolled. From there, something began to grow. We started meeting once a month and from time to time we organised simple outings together. What started as support slowly became a community.

“We started with almost nothing, a small room and a broken coffee table we had found outside. But it held our tea, our conversations, and our ideas.” Naima’s group evolved into a charity, UPLIFT in which many of the original women now work as dedicated volunteers. Coffee mornings, youth groups, fitness classes and day trips bring up to 400 people through their doors each week.

‌



“Our aim was simple: to support people facing language barriers, isolation, and the challenges of starting a new life in a different country,” Naima says. “I understood that feeling deeply. Even as someone who speaks several languages, I know what it feels like not to be understood. I did not want that for anyone else.”

6 View 6 Images Justin Pearson turned to Hatfield Foodbank for support after losing daughter Skye (Image: Supplied) 6 View 6 Images Heather Dyce, trustee of Hatfield Foodbank. (Image: Supplied)

In Hatfield, Herts, we met Justin Pearson, a bereaved father who lost his beloved daughter Skye aged eight to sepsis in 2018. Skye had Downs Syndrome and a rare congenital heart defect that led to nine cardiac arrests. Battling with their mental health, the 52-year-old former farmworker and his wife have struggled to work since, meaning they sometimes need the help of the local foodbank.

‌



“When my daughter passed away, it ripped our family apart,” Justin said. "I should have walked my daughter down the aisle, not carried her down one. I went back to work but didn’t realise I was having a breakdown. I collapsed at work, I became very, very poorly. As our life stumbled, and we struggled to move forward, we had to seek support from Hatfield Foodbank. They welcomed us.

“It wasn’t just the food that made a difference to us, it was the fact they showed such empathy and care for us in our very darkest moments. That’s special.”

In Cardiff, we spoke to 36-year-old Rhys Holmes, who had a brain tumour removed when he was just eight years old, and then became ill with meningitis, and later a neurodegenerative disorder called superficial siderosis. As a child Rhys had been a promising footballer, scouted by Cardiff, but his health problems saw him drop out of sport and his music degree. He had to learn to walk again and had a cochlear implant fitted. He attends weekly neuro-physiotherapy.

View 6 Images Rhys Holmes, who had a brain tumour removed aged 8, on his ICE Trike at Pedal Power, Cardiff.

‌



Some 23 surgeries later, Rhys is a keen cyclist, and trustee of Pedal Power, an inclusive cycling project run from a hub at Cardiff Caravan Park. He has his own ICE Trike, and leads one of the weekly recumbent trike social rides. “I was very active when I was younger but doctors said I couldn’t continue with football, as my head was too fragile,” Rhys says. “My dad bought me a guitar to compensate, and my love for music and doing gigs grew from there.

“But after getting diagnosed with superficial siderosis, I became very isolated. I couldn’t hear for five years. I stopped working, I lost friends and my confidence. It was the worst time of my life, it was horrendous. My mum drove me to my first Pedal Power session, and it has changed my life.”

In Greater Manchester we spoke to Becky Goodwin, who runs the Mencap project ‘Me Time Tameside’ – which recently moved from an isolated industrial estate into local community hubs. Being part of A Million Acts of Hope feels incredibly meaningful for everyone at Mencap Me Time Tameside,” she says. "The one simple change of moving into the heart of Tameside has created countless hopeful moments. These everyday moments of connection and belonging are exactly what A Million Acts of Hope is about.”

James Bowes, 36, says: "Mencap Tameside has helped me a lot. When I first started I was the shyest one ever. I have enjoyed being with everyone and liked it so much. I’ve changed a lot. I love it here – If I had a bed I would put it here and live here!"

‌



View 6 Images Service users from Mencap Tameside who supports people with learning disabilities.

Back on the Buttershaw, the chairwoman of Recycled Teenagers, Anne Newsome, 71, tells us about the wisdom of long life. “We’ve all lived, we’ve all been there and done it and now we’re doing our bit to share and help others,” Anne says. “I’ll never forget seeing a mum with tears rolling down her cheeks because we’d given her Christmas presents to take home. She didn’t think her children were going to have anything to open so what we’d done, it meant the world. She was crying, then I was. I’ll never forget that - that’s what it’s all about.”
